one_liner: Scalar C byte-histogram routines for entropy-coder front ends; 1.5x the naive loop on text, up to 22x on runs.
what_it_does: Counts the 256 byte frequencies of a buffer, the first pass of Huffman, FSE/tANS and rANS encoders. Each routine has the shape f(unsigned char *in, unsigned inlen, unsigned *cnt) and fills a 256-entry 32-bit count array. There is no library or header: the functions are static functions in turbohist_.c, included by the turbohist.c benchmark driver, so you copy the one you want into your code.
how_it_is_fast: It spreads increments over 4 or 8 separate count tables so consecutive equal bytes do not serialize on a store-to-load forwarding dependency, then sums the tables at the end in an auto-vectorizable loop. It reads 32- or 64-bit words and extracts bytes with shifts (x86 uses the high-byte trick via unsigned short casts), prefetches 512 bytes ahead, and pads each table to 256+8 counters to avoid 4K aliasing between tables (issue #2). The histr_* variants compare two 64-bit words and, when 16 bytes are one repeated value, add 16 to a single counter, which is where the 19.6 GB/s all-zeros figure comes from.
when_to_use: The counting pass in front of a block entropy coder (Huffman, FSE, rANS) on blocks of KB to GB, single thread
Skewed or run-heavy data (BWT output, sparse images, zero-filled regions): histr_8_64 measured 5135 MB/s vs 1171 MB/s naive on enwik9.bwt and 19629 vs 877 MB/s on zeros
Portable C without SIMD or assembly requirements: the fastest rows are plain scalar C, so the same code serves x86-64, aarch64 and ppc64le builds
As a reference when tuning your own histogram loop: the driver checks every variant against the naive count and reports MB/s and cycles/byte
when_not_to_use: Uniform, high-entropy data where the gain is modest: on enwik9 text hist_8_64 is 4053 MB/s vs 2761 MB/s naive (about 1.47x, derived from page data)
Inputs of 4 GiB or more in one call, or counts above 2^32-1: lengths and counters are 32-bit unsigned

Small buffers (a few hundred bytes): each call zeroes and later sums 8 x 264 counters (about 8.4 KB of stack), which can outweigh the counting; the 64-bit variants only enter the fast loop for inlen >= 72-80 bytes
Multi-threaded or 16-bit-symbol histograms: only single-thread 8-bit symbol counting is implemented
Projects that need a maintained, versioned library: no releases, no header, last commit 2021-12-29

integration.dependencies: none for the functions (conf.h supplies ctou32/ctou64, likely and ALWAYS_INLINE macros; sse_neon.h only for the SSE/NEON variants)
integration.min_toolchain: GCC >= 4.6 or Clang >= 3.2 on Linux, MinGW-w64 on Windows, Xcode >= 9 on macOS, gcc >= 6.3 on aarch64, gcc >= 8.0 on ppc64le (README); C99 with GCC builtins
integration.platforms: x86-64 and i386 (default build -march=corei7-avx; AVX2=1 uses -march=haswell), aarch64, Apple M1, ppc64le; hist_8_64a inline-asm variant is x86-64 only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the code keeps all count tables on the stack and has no global state, so separate calls on separate buffers do not share data
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same signature shape as a naive count loop (input, length, 256-entry counts), but you must copy the static function and the conf.h load macros

gotchas: The README advertises a 'C++ compatible header', but no header exists in the repo (turbohist.h returns 404); the functions are static in turbohist_.c.

Table rows came from a build whose flags are not stated (default -march=corei7-avx or AVX2=1 -march=haswell), so expect different ratios with other flags; the SSE4.1 and AVX2 variants were slower than the scalar 64-bit ones on the i7-9700K.
hist_8_64a is declared to return unsigned but has no return statement; do not use its return value.
The disabled '#else' table-reduction path mixes _mm256_add_epi32 with __m128i in its SSE branch and would not compile if enabled; leave the default '#if 1' summation.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The sibling entries (FiniteStateEntropy, hypersonic-rANS, htscodecs, rans_static) are coders, not histogram routines; use TurboHist as their counting stage when profiling shows the frequency pass matters, especially on BWT or run-heavy blocks where its run-aware histr_8_64 is 1.1x Ryg's best asm and 4.4x the naive loop.
verified_claims_summary: First-party single-thread benchmark on an Intel i7-9700K with gcc 11.2 over 1 GB inputs, every variant checked against the naive count: hist_8_64 4053 MB/s vs naive 2761 MB/s on enwik9, histr_8_64 5135 vs 1171 MB/s on enwik9.bwt and 19629 vs 877 MB/s on all zeros (the 22x headline). Against Ryg's assembly histograms the lead is small: 4053 vs 4133 MB/s (Ryg var3 is faster on enwik9), 5135 vs 4642 MB/s on BWT and 19629 vs 14076 MB/s on zeros.
status_note: Abandoned since 2021-12-29 (102 commits, 74 stars, no releases, no open issues) but BSD-2-Clause and a few dozen lines per function, so easy to vendor.
